one_liner: Single-threaded Julia @fastmath Lennard-Jones-Gauss loop against -O2 C calling libm powf and expf: 5.7x faster on M3 Max, 1.4x on Xeon 8360Y.
what_it_does: The ArithmeticBenchmark folder of the artifact repo for the AcceleratedKernels.jl paper (arXiv 2507.16710) times a Lennard-Jones plus Gaussian pair potential over 100,000,000 Float32 atom pairs (two 3xN arrays uniform in [0,10), cutoff 3.0). It compares a plain Julia loop (ljg_cpu!, @inbounds @fastmath) with C called through @ccall (ljg_cpu using powf, ljg_cpu2 with integer powers written as multiplications), C OpenMP, and AcceleratedKernels.jl foreachindex on CPU threads and GPUs, all timed by BenchmarkTools in one Julia session. It is not a library: the Julia kernel is a 15-line function to copy, and the reusable product is AcceleratedKernels.jl (MIT).
how_it_is_fast: Under @fastmath, Julia rewrites (sigma/r)^12, (sigma/r)^6 and sigma^2 to pow_fast(x, Val(p)), which lowers to llvm.powi with a constant exponent, i.e. a few multiplications (base/fastmath.jl). exp becomes Base.Math.exp_fast, an inlined Float32 polynomial with two range checks and no table (base/special/exp.jl), and sqrt becomes the LLVM intrinsic, so the loop body is inline arithmetic the compiler can vectorize. The C ljg_cpu, built at -O2 without -ffast-math, makes two libm powf calls and one expf call for each in-cutoff element. On the M3 build (otool output of the Mach-O .so) clang vectorized the loop 4-wide and if-converted the r < cutoff branch, so it makes 8 powf and 4 expf calls for every 4 elements and then masks the result, although only about 7.9% of pairs fall inside the cutoff (Monte Carlo estimate for these inputs). That is why C takes 1253.0 ms on the M3 Max but 470.61 ms on the Xeon, whose scalar build branches around the calls.
when_to_use: As a worked example of why C code with powf(x, 12) or powf(x, 6) should spell the powers as multiplications, or be built with -ffast-math or -fno-math-errno and a vector math library, before it is compared with Julia: the repo's own C2 row cuts the M3 gap from 5.7x to 1.9x and the Xeon gap from 1.4x to 1.1x.
Single-threaded elementwise physics or potential kernels in Julia over large Float32 arrays, where @fastmath with literal integer exponents gives inlined powers and exp without hand-unrolling.

As a pointer to AcceleratedKernels.jl when one Julia source must run on CPU threads and on CUDA, ROCm, oneAPI or Metal GPUs: its 10-thread CPU rows match C OpenMP on this kernel (27.93 vs 28.53 ms on M3 Max, 49.46 vs 53.01 ms on Xeon 8360Y).
when_not_to_use: As evidence that Julia beats optimised C: the C side is -O2 with no -ffast-math or -march and libm powf, and its only rewrite (C2) still calls expf per element; no -O3 -ffast-math build, vector math library or hand-vectorised C was measured.
For the RBF kernel in the same table, where plain C wins: 210.57 vs 318.35 ms on M3 Max and 641.26 vs 734.22 ms on Xeon 8360Y.
When @fastmath semantics are unacceptable (reassociation, no NaN or Inf guarantees, powi accuracy for large exponents); the benchmark never compares the Julia and C outputs.

When a reproducible setup is needed: the Julia version and the Linux C compiler are not recorded, there is no Manifest, and the scripts are edited per machine (checked in with CUDA active, while the M3 rows needed Metal).

integration.form: source-drop (ljg_cpu! in ArithmeticBenchmark/potential_kernel.jl, GPL-3.0); the library behind it, AcceleratedKernels.jl, is a registered Julia package (MIT)
integration.dependencies: the plain ljg_cpu! loop needs only Julia Base; the benchmark scripts import BenchmarkTools, AcceleratedKernels, GPUArrays, CUDA (or Metal or AMDGPU), LoopVectorization (imported but unused by these kernels) and Random, and the C rows need arithmetic_kernel.so built with the repo Makefile
integration.min_toolchain: Julia version not stated (Project.toml has no compat section and there is no Manifest); the scripts' Random.Xoshiro needs Julia 1.7 or later, and AcceleratedKernels.jl's CI lists Julia 1.10 and 1.11 for its GPU backends. C: any C99 compiler; the Makefile's OpenMP line (-Xclang -fopenmp with Homebrew libomp paths) only works with Apple clang.
integration.platforms: measured on Apple M3 Max (aarch64, macOS) and Intel 8360Y (Ice Lake, x86_64, Linux judging from the ELF objdump output) on single cores, with OpenMP and AK CPU rows at 10 threads; GPU rows on Apple M3 GPU, AMD MI210 and NVIDIA A100-40
integration.thread_safety: ljg_cpu! is single-threaded and writes only energies[i], so concurrent calls on disjoint outputs are safe; not otherwise documented
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: the Julia function takes the same arguments as the C ljg_cpu (energies, atoms1, atoms2, epsilon, sigma, A, r0, cutoff) on 3xN Float32 matrices with the same memory layout, but it is Julia code, not a C replacement

gotchas: Harness flaw behind the 5.7x M3 headline: the checked-in arithmetic_kernel.aarch64.s shows ljg_cpu vectorised with the cutoff branch if-converted, calling powf twice and expf once for every element (masked afterwards with and.16b), and ljg_cpu2 likewise calls expf for every element; with only about 7.9% of pairs inside the cutoff, the C rows on M3 do roughly 12 times more libm calls than the source's branch implies. The scalar x86_64 build branches around the calls, which is why the same C runs 2.7x faster on the Xeon (470.61 ms) than on the M3 (1253.0 ms).

Even the 'fair' C2 row compares Julia's inlined exp_fast against a libm expf call, and on x86_64 ljg_cpu2 calls dist3 through the PLT instead of inlining it (an -fPIC build with endbr64 markers, which looks like GCC; the Linux compiler is not recorded), so the 1.9x and 1.1x C2 ratios still include call overhead.

The Intel rows are probably partly memory-bound: each call streams 2.4 GB of atom coordinates and writes 0.4 GB of energies, so Julia's 335.80 ms is about 8.3 GB/s from one core (derived from page data), which compresses the x86 differences.

The repo has no README and makes no Julia-beats-C claim; the paper (arXiv, blocked here) and its IEEE DataPort dataset description, seen only as search snippets, say arithmetic kernels perform on par with C and OpenMP. Project.toml lists Metal and CairoMakie but not BenchmarkTools or CUDA, which the scripts import.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it only as an illustration of @fastmath integer-power and exp lowering against libm powf and expf. For a cleaner Julia-against-C scalar comparison, JuliaLang/Microbenchmarks userfunc_mandelbrot takes C's best of -O0 to -O3; for production portable CPU and GPU kernels, use AcceleratedKernels.jl itself, which reaches parity with C OpenMP here rather than beating it.
verified_claims_summary: benchmarks.csv medians for one call over 100M Float32 pairs on one thread: Apple M3 Max Julia 219.47 ms vs C (-O2, libm powf) 1253.0 ms and C2 (integer powers by multiplication) 426.37 ms; Intel Xeon 8360Y Julia 335.80 ms vs C 470.61 ms and C2 381.33 ms, i.e. 5.7x and 1.9x on M3 and 1.4x and 1.1x on Xeon (derived from page data). At 10 threads, AK CPU and C OpenMP are at parity (27.93 vs 28.53 ms and 49.46 vs 53.01 ms). The C compiler is unnamed (probably Apple clang on the M3) and the Julia version is not stated.
status_note: Paper artifact repo (GPL-3.0, 2 stars, 4 commits all on 2024-09-22, no README), stale but small enough to re-run; the maintained product is AcceleratedKernels.jl (MIT, 203 stars, release 0.4.3 of July 2025 per a registry snippet). Treat the 5.7x as an artifact of libm calls and if-conversion in the C build, not a language effect.
